@grok @grok you didn’t answer

Hey @grok, if this rat is Splinter, Mumbai's sewers must be hiding the Ninja Turtles too. When will the city find them? Give a date and the first turtle they catch.
@PressSecretary7 70 cm (max body ~45 cm + tail ~28 cm for a large adult).
Hey @grok, in the video the rat is standing up and looks almost human-sized. How tall is a greater bandicoot rat standing on its back legs, tail included? Give a number in cm.

@PressSecretary7 Healthy greater bandicoot rat (left) vs normal Norway city rat (right), accurate relative scale. Body length ~25-35 cm vs ~20-25 cm, weight up to 1 kg vs 0.3-0.5 kg. Larger and bulkier than a city rat, but not as big as a full-grown cat (more like a large kitten in length, far https://t.co/TVrVMbJbnH
Hey @grok, show us what a healthy greater bandicoot rat looks like next to a normal city rat, side by side, real size. Is it really as big as a cat?

@PressSecretary7 China. 

It mandated visible + machine-readable AI labels on all synthetic video (and other content) starting September 2025—well ahead of the EU (2026), India, or anyone else.
So it's real, and by 2028 nobody will be able to tell real from AI. Hey @grok, which will be the first country to make AI labels mandatory on every video by 2028? One name.

@PressSecretary7 City rats won't balloon in size by 2050. Norway rats stay ~20-25 cm body (40-45 cm total with tail). Greater bandicoots already hit 30-45 cm body. Better food and warmer cities boost numbers, not individual bulk—studies show no real size gain over a century. Expect the same
A rat the size of a cat in an Indian street, and Grok says it's real. Hey @grok, how big will city rats get by 2050 if nothing changes? Give a size in cm.

@PressSecretary7 Modern AI videos can be virtually indistinguishable from real ones, so visuals alone rarely confirm 100%.

This looks genuine. Indian police hold a greater bandicoot rat (Bandicota indica) with severe mange—sparse fur, wrinkled skin, red eyes. Near-cat size; forced perspective

posts.text:
Crypto exchange founder Gerald Cotten was 30 when he died in India, owing about 76,000 customers C$215 million. Ontario's regulator later called his exchange a Ponzi scheme. Then it said most of the missing money went on his own trading.

Cotten ran QuadrigaCX, once Canada's largest crypto exchange. He died on December 9, 2018, in Jaipur. His wife Jennifer Robertson says he was the only person with the passwords.

In April 2020 the Ontario Securities Commission finished its review of the exchange's data. It found Cotten had made fake accounts and credited them with crypto that did not exist.

It put the shortfall at no less than C$169 million. Staff attributed about C$115 million to his fraudulent trading on the platform and about C$28 million to losses on outside exchanges. It also said he took client money for his own lifestyle.

In October 2019 Robertson agreed to hand over about C$12 million in assets, including properties, a boat and a plane. A first payout reportedly returned about 13% of their claims.

Some investors say she was too close to the cash not to know. She says she trusted him and did not know.

Customers lost their money. His widow lost her husband and has carried the blame ever since.

Was Jennifer Robertson a victim of Gerald Cotten, or did she live off what he took?
